# Follow the Money: Why Outsiders in Both Parties Are Fighting the Same Fight

A plain-language summary of the Minnesota campaign money analysis August 17, 2026 · Every
number comes from public campaign finance records — Minnesota Campaign Finance Board
filings (2015–2026) and federal FEC filings for the 2026 Senate race.

## The short version

If you look at where campaign money actually comes from — not what candidates say, but who
writes the checks — Minnesota politics doesn't divide into Republicans versus Democrats. It
divides into **insiders versus outsiders**, and that line cuts straight through both parties.

The outsider candidates in the Republican party and the outsider candidates in the DFL are
funded almost identically: small donations from regular people and their local county party.
The insider candidates in both parties are also funded almost identically: PACs, lobbyists,
and party machinery — and often by **the exact same PACs and lobbyists**.

The two party establishments have more in common with each other than either one has with its
own grassroots. That's not an opinion. It's arithmetic.

## Where the money actually goes

Here's the first surprise: most political money in Minnesota never touches a candidate.

Over the last eleven years, all 1,700-or-so candidates for state office **combined** raised
about $108 million. Meanwhile, the four legislative caucus committees and the two state
parties took in about **$221 million** — twice as much. And another **$179 million** was
spent "independently" on ads and mail *about* candidates, money the candidates never see and
can't control. More than half of that independent money was spent attacking someone rather
than supporting anyone.

So the candidate on your ballot is usually the *smallest* financial player in their own race.
The real money sits one level up, in the party machinery — and whoever funds the machinery has
more influence than any donor to any candidate.

And the biggest money of all isn't in elections. Companies and organizations spent **$886
million lobbying** the Minnesota government since 2015 — more than all candidates, caucuses,
and parties combined.

## The same donors fund both parties

Now the part almost nobody knows.

We checked every organization — PACs, lobbying firms, trade groups, unions — that gives to
the party machinery. **345 of them give to both parties.** Together they supply almost
**half** of all the organizational money flowing into the Republican and DFL apparatus. Among
the big funders (over $10,000), **53% fund both sides**.

One small example: an optometrists' PAC gave the Republican caucuses about $57,000 and the
DFL caucuses about $67,000. A power company's employee PAC split its giving almost to the
dollar: $139,649 to one side, $137,914 to the other. Law firms, realtors, hospitals, beer
wholesalers, banks — the list runs to hundreds.

Think about what even-money giving means. Nobody splits their donations 50/50 because they
believe in both parties' opposite ideas. You split 50/50 when you're **betting on both horses**
— buying a relationship with whoever wins. That's not left money or right money. It's access
money, and it's the largest single source of funding for both establishments.

Regular people don't do this. Ordinary Minnesota donors cross party lines about 12% of the time.
The big institutional funders do it 53% of the time. **The most bipartisan group in Minnesota
politics is the money.**

## The outsiders look the same — in both parties

We scored every candidate committee that raised at least $20,000 since 2021 on how it was
funded: how much came from PACs, how much from small donors, how much from local party
volunteers, and whether their donors were professionals who fund a hundred committees or
neighbors who fund one or two.

The result: **outsider candidates in the two parties are about four times more similar to each
other than to their own party's establishment.** And the two establishments? They're the most
similar pair of all.

The clearest single number is what we call donor breadth. An establishment candidate's average
dollar comes from someone who funds **80 to 150 different political committees** — professional
political money. An outsider's average dollar comes from someone who funds about **a dozen** —
a real person who cares about a few things. Those are two entirely different worlds of money,
and the divide between them ignores the party line completely.

One more detail worth knowing: outsider candidates actually get **more** support from their local
county and district party organizations than establishment candidates do. The neighbors who run
the local party and the professionals who run the state apparatus are not the same people — and
they back different candidates.

## Small money versus big money — the honest math

- Donations of $200 or less make up about **2%** of all itemized campaign money.
- The top 5% of candidates hold nearly **60%** of everything all candidates ever raised.
- The typical candidate raised about **$13,000 total over eleven years**. The machinery moved
  hundreds of millions.

For a normal competitive legislative race, roughly **40 to 46 cents of every dollar** the
candidate raises comes from PACs, lobbyists, and party organizations — before counting the
independent ads spent around them.

One district tells the whole story. In Senate District 13, the sitting senator raised just
$9,025 — but 82% of it came from PACs, from donors who fund 148 committees each. The
party-endorsed candidate raised his money from the county party and small gifts — zero PAC
dollars — and lost. The challenger who beat him got a modest amount directly, plus **$58,000 in
outside ads** paid for by a fund that is 99% financed by the state Chamber of Commerce — eight
times what his own campaign spent. The voters saw three names. The money saw three completely
different candidates.

## The Senate race: three candidates, three kinds of money

The 2026 U.S. Senate race shows that "establishment" isn't one thing. We pulled the raw federal
filings for all the major candidates:

**Angie Craig** skipped the party convention and ran against the endorsed candidate — which
*sounds* like an outsider move. Her money says otherwise: nearly $10 million, about half her
individual money from donors giving the legal maximum, $1.8 million from PACs, plus transfers
from her old campaign accounts and a $373,000 personal loan. She used institutional money to go
*around* the institution's process. She lost.

**Peggy Flanagan** was the party's chosen candidate — endorsed at the convention, backed by
eight U.S. senators. But her *money* looks like an outsider's: median donation $30, only 6% from
committees. The party picked her, and regular people funded her. She won — beating a 3-to-1
money disadvantage.

**Michele Tafoya** is the newest wrinkle. Her donors look genuinely grassroots — median gift $50,
13% of her money in gifts under $100, and the most Minnesota-based donor list of the three. But
the **national** Republican Party in Washington sent her $62,000 in early February — six months
*before* the primary, while the **state** party's endorsed candidate was still running — followed
by about $213,000 from U.S. senators' leadership PACs. She beat the state establishment's
candidate with the national establishment's help.

The lesson: there isn't one establishment. There are at least **three layers** — your local party
volunteers, the state apparatus, and Washington — and the records show them backing *different
candidates in the same race*. Any honest picture of a campaign has to show all three separately.

## Why the outsiders can't see each other

Here's the part that answers "why hasn't anyone noticed?"

We matched donor lists across the party line (carefully — by name *and* ZIP code, because sloppy
matching produces mostly false hits). Outsider candidates' donors cross party lines at a rate of
**less than 1%** — far below even ordinary partisan donors. The big institutions cross at 53%.

So the two groups of outsiders share **no fundraisers, no consultants, no mailing lists, no
rooms**. A DFL outsider fighting the DFL apparatus and a Republican outsider fighting the
Republican apparatus are having *the same fight against the same kind of opponent* — but the
only thing each can see about the other is policy, so each codes the other as the enemy.

**The similarity is in the plumbing, and nobody looks at the plumbing.** The people funding
both establishments can see the whole board. The people funding the outsiders can only see their
own square.

## What this means for an independent movement — the honest version

This is where we owe you straight talk, because the obvious conclusion isn't quite right.

**What the data supports:** outsiders in both parties really do share something — a critique of
*how the system works*. Concentrated money, party machinery that picks winners before voters
do, institutions that answer to their funders. That complaint is measurably justified. The 53%
both-sides funding figure is the receipt.

**What the data does not support:** that they secretly agree on policy. They don't — their donor
bases are the most separated groups we measured. A movement built on "we hate the same machine"
and nothing else tends to fall apart the day after it wins.

**And one myth to retire:** third parties in Minnesota are not being starved out by money. All
minor parties combined took in $1.5 million over eleven years — two-thirds of one percent of
what the party machinery took in — but nobody is blocking them. Minnesota is actually generous:
easy ballot access, a state refund program that subsidizes small-party donors, and a governor's
mansion that an independent (Jesse Ventura) actually won. The real wall is the voting system
itself — winner-take-all elections mathematically squeeze everything toward two parties.
**The independent lane isn't locked. It's open and empty.**

So why does an independent movement still matter? Because it's the only place the shared fight
can become visible. Inside the parties, the outsiders will always be told the enemy is across
the aisle. The one thing both sides' outsiders could actually build together isn't a policy
platform — it's **transparency**: making the money visible so every voter can see who funds the
machinery, which layer of which party picked which candidate, and whether their representative
is funded by neighbors or by professionals who fund 148 committees.

That's a project both a MAGA voter and a DSA voter can check with their own eyes, because it
isn't an argument. It's a lookup.

## The one rule this whole analysis follows

We never claim to know *why* anyone gave money. A PAC funding both parties is a fact; what it
wants in return is a question. A national party check dated six months before a primary is a
fact; what was promised is unknown. Some candidates called extremists are extremists; some
outsiders lose because they're bad candidates — no spreadsheet can tell you which.

So we don't fight about labels. We publish the numbers — who gave, to whom, how much, and when
— with a link to the official filing, and let you decide. A candidate whose donors fund 2
committees and a candidate whose donors fund 148 is a fact nobody can call extreme.

Everything above comes from public records anyone can check. The point of Alethical is to make
checking take five minutes instead of five months.

2026 primary results. Full technical version with all figures, methods, and caveats: "The
